target_customer: Smartphone owners who wanted to share photos and updates privately with specific groups of friends and family, using their address book
problem: Public social networks made people worry about who saw what, and getting everyone to join a new service was hard. Everyme let a user post to private Circles built from the phone address book, with non-members reachable by email or text.
business_model: Free consumer social app, no revenue model reported
product_category: Private social network and group messaging app

founders.name: Oliver Cameron
founders.background_notes: The YC page bio says he later became CEO of Odyssey and earlier worked on self-driving cars. No education or pre-2011 employers found in opened sources.

founders.name: Vibhu Norby
founders.background_notes: TechCrunch (Oct 2011) calls him a former MySpace engineer. YC page lists him as founder of Everyme, Origami (YC S11) and later b8ta.

exit.reason: The spin-off Origami was sold to eFamily in November 2013 and its six-person team was acqui-hired by Nest. What happened to the Everyme app itself is not stated.

competitors.name: Plaxo
competitors.what: Online address book that syncs and updates contacts

competitors.name: Xobni
competitors.what: Smart address book and inbox contact tool

technical_complexity.rationale: A mobile and web app built on the phone address book with email and SMS bridging to non-users. Standard engineering for a two person team in 2011, with no research-grade parts.

defensibility.rationale: Private group sharing was copyable by Facebook, Google+ and Path, and the only claimed edge was a privacy promise and address-book onboarding.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Facebook groups and Google+ circles already covered private sharing. TechCrunch later described Everyme as a messaging and photo app that never really took off.

market_need_then: Privacy worries about public social networks and Google+ circles launching in 2011 showed interest in audience control. Everyme reported about 200,000 people in 17,000 circles shortly after its April 2012 iPhone launch (TNW, April 2012), which is after the batch.

branding.domain_note: everyme.com was the company domain. It now redirects to a GoDaddy for-sale page (observed Nov 2026).

identity.logo: Everyme wordmark, catalogued on Fonts In Use in April 2012 as copyright Everyme, Inc.
identity.voice_and_tone: Privacy first, framed as sharing like in real life

branding.brand_signature: The Circles feature, described as a private news feed with a chosen group
branding.community_and_virality: Press coverage at launch in April 2012 by TechCrunch, TNW and Daring Fireball linked posts. No merch or fan community found.

brand_strength.rationale: Launch coverage was strong but the name was easy to confuse with EverythingMe, a different startup, and the service did not take off.

pivots.to: Origami, a private sharing service for families
pivots.why: Everyme did not gain traction as a general private network, so the team launched a family focused spin-off.

outcome_analysis: Everyme raised about 1.5 million dollars in October 2011 from a strong investor group but launched its app only in April 2012, then spun out Origami for families in 2013. TechCrunch said Everyme never really took off and that raising another round looked hard, so the team sold Origami in November 2013 and joined Nest. Facebook and Google+ already served private group sharing.
notes: Total raised is stated as 3.66 million dollars by TechCrunch (Nov 2013), so the two recorded rounds (3.65 million) roughly cover it. The 2012 round rests on a single database (CB Insights labels it Series A II, other aggregators give totals of 3.67 to 3.79 million); no investors recorded. TechCrunch 2011 does not label the 2011 round, so stage is other. Website is dead (parked for sale). Status Inactive; exit type is unknown because only the Origami spin-off sale is documented. The dealroom/parsers pages that say Everyme was acquired by eFamily rest on one aggregator and conflict with TechCrunch, which says Origami was sold.
